classification.difficultyReason: Choose parallel-line constructions that preserve areas, then compose two vertex-elimination operations to turn a general convex pentagon into a triangle.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral. A line through the vertex $A$, parallel to the diagonal $BD$, meets $CD$ (extended) at $E$. Show that the area of triangle $BCE$ equals the area of $ABCD$.

answer.worked:
The vertices $A$ and $E$ lie on a line parallel to $BD$, so triangles $ABD$ and $EBD$ have the same base $BD$ and the same perpendicular height. Thus $[ABD]=[EBD]$. Since $C,D,E$ are collinear with $D$ between $C$ and $E$,
$$\begin{aligned}[BCE]&=[BCD]+[BDE]\\&=[BCD]+[ABD]\\&=[ABCD].\end{aligned}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Let $ABCDE$ be a convex pentagon. Construct a triangle with the same area as this pentagon.

answer.short: Construct $P$ on $CD$ produced with $BP\parallel AC$. Then construct $Q$ on $DE$ produced with $AQ\parallel PE$. Triangle $PDQ$ has the required area.
answer.worked:
Draw diagonal $AC$. Through $B$ draw a line parallel to $AC$, meeting $CD$ produced beyond $C$ at $P$. Triangles $ABC$ and $APC$ have equal area, sharing base $AC$ with their third vertices on a parallel line. Replacing triangle $ABC$ by $APC$ turns convex pentagon $ABCDE$ into equal-area quadrilateral $APDE$.

Apply part a to quadrilateral $APDE$: through $A$ draw a line parallel to diagonal $PE$, meeting $DE$ produced at $Q$. Triangle $PDQ$ has the area of $APDE$, hence the original pentagon. Keep the construction lines and mark both pairs of parallel lines.
